opus-5.5.text:
I think the interesting thing is that when we answer a question about an object, we often assume the hard part is language: parsing the question, retrieving knowledge, producing an answer. But a lot of the real work happens before any of that, in how you actually *look* at the thing.

Say I show you a picture of a mug on a cluttered desk and ask, "Can this hold hot coffee?" To answer, you first have to find the mug, separate it from the background, notice whether it has a handle, whether it's ceramic or paper, maybe whether there's a crack in it. That's not just recognition, where you say "this is a mug" and you're done. It's a sequence of perceptual steps where you decide where to attend next based on what you've already seen and what the question needs. To me, that is visual reasoning: reasoning that happens in visual space, not only reasoning that happens after you've converted the image into words.

A lot of current multimodal systems compress the image into a fixed set of tokens once, up front, and then all the "thinking" happens in the language model. That works surprisingly well for many benchmarks, but it means the model can't really go back and look again. Humans don't work like that. When something is ambiguous, we zoom in, we shift our gaze, we compare two regions. The question shapes the looking, and the looking reshapes how we understand the question.

So when I think about visual reasoning as part of answering a question about an object, I think about a loop: perception that's driven by intent, and intent that's updated by perception. It's spatial, it's about relationships, about 3D structure, about physical properties you can infer but can't read off a label. And honestly, I think this is one of the places where vision still lags behind language. We've gotten very good at describing images. We're not yet as good at *thinking with* images. Closing that gap is, I think, one of the most important problems for the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes visual reasoning as a sequence of perceptual steps—such as finding and inspecting the mug—used to answer a question about it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that visual reasoning, when you ask a question about an object, is really the process of figuring out what you need to look at and then actually looking there. A lot of what happens in current multimodal models is that you give the model an image, you encode it once into a fixed set of tokens, and then everything after that is essentially language reasoning over a frozen summary of the picture. That works for a surprising number of questions, but it's not really visual reasoning. It's more like reading a caption and reasoning about the caption.

So if I ask you something like, "is this cup chipped on the rim," a human doesn't answer from a global impression. You look at the cup, you find the rim, you maybe mentally zoom in, you trace around it, you compare one side to the other. The question actually changes how you perceive the object. The reasoning drives the perception, not just the other way around. And I think that's the crux of it: visual reasoning means perception should be an active, iterative thing that is conditioned on what you're trying to answer.

For me there are a few pieces to this. One is the representation itself. If the visual encoder throws away fine-grained spatial information, geometry, material, the little details, then no amount of reasoning on top will recover it. That's partly why I've been interested in encoders that are trained with stronger visual objectives rather than only language alignment. The second piece is that the model should be able to go back to the image. Re-attend, crop, zoom, compare regions, count things step by step, instead of committing to one pass. Chain-of-thought in text is useful, but for questions about objects I think you want something closer to chain-of-thought in the visual space, where intermediate steps are grounded in actual pixels.

And the third piece, honestly, is that a lot of the questions we care about are about the physical world, not about language. Where is the object relative to other things, how big is it, what would happen if I rotated it, is this the same object from a different angle. Language models have very little pretraining signal for that kind of thing. So when I say "visual reasoning about an object," I'm also pointing at this gap: the model needs some internal sense of space and objects that it builds up from vision itself, and then language is the interface for asking and answering, not the substrate where all the thinking happens.

r001.rationale: The response defines visual reasoning as figuring out what to inspect and looking there while answering an object question, with perception guided by the question.

astra-6.text:
I think visual reasoning means more than recognizing what an object is. If you ask, “Can this cup hold water?” identifying it as a cup is only the first step. You also need to look at its condition: is there a crack, does it have a bottom, is it upside down? Then you connect that visual evidence with what you know about how objects work.

So the question determines what you need to see. You might look at the overall scene, form a hypothesis, and then look more closely at a particular detail to check it. In that sense, perception and reasoning are intertwined. The challenge is to make sure the answer follows from the object actually in front of you, rather than just from what is usually true of objects in that category.

r001.rationale: The response explains that answering an object question involves inspecting relevant visual details and reasoning from them, describing this as perception and reasoning intertwined.

sol-6.1.text:
I think visual reasoning starts with understanding what the question actually requires you to see. If you ask, “What color is this object?” that’s mostly recognition. But if you ask, “Can this cup hold more water?” you need to consider its shape, whether it’s already full, maybe even whether it has a hole. You’re connecting visual evidence with knowledge about how the world works.

So the object isn’t just a label. You need to understand its properties, its relationship to other things, and which of those details matter for answering the question. And sometimes the right answer is that the image doesn’t give you enough information. Knowing that boundary is also part of visual reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response describes visual reasoning as examining relevant visual evidence and connecting it to world knowledge to answer questions about an object.
